The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be "in Christ" is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: "be transformed by the renewal of your mind." The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is "the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in His image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I say and testify in the Lord” — that second word is heavier than it looks. The Greek is martyromai, from martys, “witness” — the root that gives us martyr. It belongs to the solemn, legal register: to call something to witness, to affirm it as under oath. Paul is not offering friendly advice; he is swearing a charge, staking his own witness on it. And that he must issue it at all tells us something: conversion does not automatically make us live as God wills. The old patterns do not vanish overnight; the new life must be deliberately walked.

“No longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.” “Futility” (mataiotēs) means emptiness — the very word the Old Testament uses for idols, “vain things” that cannot see or save or satisfy (Jer. 2:5); and “mind” (nous) is the whole faculty by which a person weighs what is real and decides how to live. So the diagnosis is exact: not merely muddled thinking, but a mind whose every judgment is bent because the thing at its centre is empty. Paul writes to Ephesus, built around the temple of Artemis — a life of praying to stone, buying charms, paying astrologers (Acts 19:19), busy and even religious, but aimed at gods who were not there. And there is the madness of it: a man can pour out his whole life — his worship, his labour, his deepest longing — upon what is, in truth, nothing at all.

Underneath it is a hunger. God made the heart for himself, and, as Augustine prayed, “our heart is restless until it rests in you.” We try to fill that ache with good things — family, work, a hard-earned holiday — gifts of God, every one, but never built to carry the weight of it. This is the whole burden of Ecclesiastes: the Preacher tried pleasure, work, wealth, wisdom, and called it all “vanity” (hevel, a vapour you cannot hold) — and when the book was put into Greek, that refrain was rendered with this very word, mataiotēs. Good things chased without God come up empty. Only the idols have changed clothes: the bigger house, the endless scroll, the next achievement that was finally going to satisfy — plenty of motion, no destination.

And none of this stops at conversion. You are redeemed, and you still catch yourself reaching for the old empty wells, half-believing the next thing will fill you. How do you fight it? Not mainly by gritting your teeth to want less — a hungry heart is not talked out of eating. Thomas Chalmers named the real cure: “the expulsive power of a new affection.” You do not drive out a lesser love by willpower but by a greater one. So when the itch comes — if I just had that, I’d be content — name it: that is the hunger again, and that thing cannot fill it. Preach the truth back to yourself before the craving talks you into it (the daily renewal of the mind, Rom. 12:2). Feed the real hunger at its only true source — the Word, prayer, the Lord’s table, God’s people. And receive the good gifts — your spouse, your work, your Saturday rest — not as gods that must satisfy, but as gifts from a Father who already has.

Set this diagnosis beside its cure and the contrast is exact — Paul even uses the same word. Here the Gentile mind (nous) is futile; to the Romans he pleads, “be transformed by the renewal of your mind” — the renewal of the nous (cf. Rom. 12:2). Same faculty, opposite destinies: what is empty here is the very thing grace makes new. And the renewed mind, Paul adds, now thinks “with sober judgment” (Rom. 12:3) — clear-eyed before God and self, the exact reverse of the darkened, self-deceived understanding of the next verse. The gospel does not merely correct the empty mind; it renews it.

One last thing changes how the whole command feels. You can hear “you must no longer walk” as nothing but duty — I’ve been given much, so I’d better shape up. But God is not calling you out of a good life into a grey one of chores. He is calling you out of the empty life into the full one. The walk Paul commands is not the price of being saved; it is the beauty of it — the life the heart was actually made for. The old way looked like freedom and proved a cage; this way looks like surrender and proves to be the open field (cf. Rom. 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul traces a chain, and the little joining words (“because of the ignorance… due to the hardness”) run from the surface down to the root: the darkened understanding is the visible symptom; beneath it, alienation from the life of God; beneath that, a wilful ignorance; and at the bottom, a hardened heart. The engine, though, runs the other way — the heart hardens first, and everything else follows downstream. This is not random moral failure but the predictable anatomy of a life moving away from God.

Darkened in their understanding — and the form is passive: not that they darkened themselves, but that they have been darkened; behind every eye a man closes against the light stands a judgment he did not administer. This is not stupidity — these people may be brilliant. It is the faculty by which a person decides what is worth living for, so that the needle still swings confidently but points the wrong way. Back then it looked respectable: a man pouring his years into status and the favour of Artemis, and every neighbour nodding that he lived wisely — aimed all the while at gods who were not there. And it looks just as respectable now: a decent, hard-working man pouring his one life into the career, the retirement number, the renovated house, the evenings handed to a screen — nothing scandalous, all reasonable, much of it aimed at a horizon that ends at the grave, while Christ quietly seems optional (Rom. 1:21; 2 Cor. 4:4).

And Paul has already prayed the cure for this exact darkness. To the same church, in the same letter, he asked God to grant “the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know the hope to which he has called you” (cf. Eph. 1:18). Here the understanding is darkened; there the eyes of the heart are enlightened — the same faculty of sight, opposite conditions. And note who throws the switch: not the mind lighting itself, but the Father giving light. The god of this age blinds (2 Cor. 4:4); the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” is the One who shines in the heart (2 Cor. 4:6). What sin darkened, grace floods with day.

But do not draw the wrong conclusion. Paul is not saying work and family are “worldly stuff” that does not matter, as though only church and evangelism counted with God — that is not in the Bible. God invented work before sin entered (Gen. 2:15) and called marriage and family good (Gen. 1:28). The cure was never to do less. The compass was the problem, not the road. Take the very same Monday and change the aim: do the work “as for the Lord and not for men” (Col. 3:23), love your family as a trust rather than a monument to yourself, eat and drink and clock in “all to the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10:31). To the neighbour over the fence nothing looks different; underneath, everything is — the same hands at the same tasks, no longer trying to fill the God-shaped space, but offered back to the God who already fills it.

Alienated from the life of God — there are two kinds of life. There is the life you can measure, breath and heartbeat, which every person has. And there is the deeper life: God’s own life flowing into a soul, the inner man awake and joined to its Maker. Picture a flower cut for the table: on Monday it looks perfect, bright and upright — but cut from its root it is already dying; it simply has not shown yet. That is a person alienated from the life of God — up and about, laughing, working, while cut off from the Root. “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5). And this is the very thing Christ came to reverse: the borrowed heartbeat of a cut flower gives way to life drawn again from the Root — not bare existence, but “life… to the full” (cf. John 10:10).

Beneath that lies ignorance — not for lack of information but the willed not-knowing of a man who keeps shutting his eyes against the sun and then complains that it is night (Rom. 1:21). And at the root, hardness of heart — pōrōsis, a medical word for calcification, hard tissue forming where there should be living flexibility. It is not one dramatic rebellion but the accumulation of small refusals, each making the next easier. Pharaoh is the case study, and the two halves must be held together: again and again he hardened his own heart, and again and again the LORD hardened it — the man hardened himself until God confirmed him in the hardness he had chosen. That is the most frightening sentence a soul can receive: not lightning, but a handing-over, God ceasing to interrupt. Which is why Scripture pleads, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Heb. 3:7–13).

The end of that road is a conscience worn smooth — callous, no longer feeling what it has lost — so that they “give themselves up to sensuality” (aselgeia, appetite with the brakes removed) and grow “greedy to practise every kind of impurity.” The word for greedy (pleonexia) tells the truth of it: indulgence does not satisfy, it inflames; the one who thought freedom lay in removing every limit finds himself enslaved to cravings that cannot be fed (Rom. 1:28).

And here, at the root, is the sweetest reversal of all. A heart can harden itself, but it cannot soften itself — calcified tissue does not choose to become supple again. So God pledges to do the one thing the sinner cannot: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (cf. Ezek. 36:26). Not a hard heart lectured into softness, but a new heart given. And because the hardened heart was the engine of the whole descent, when grace turns the root the rest turns with it — the darkened mind, the alienation, the very ignorance answered at a stroke. From a new heart flows a new life.

For you, this chain is a warning, not just a description. None of it begins with a dramatic fall; it begins quietly — a little hardness, a little less sensitivity, a little more drift. The Christian reads it with recognition, not superiority: this was the road we were on. Grace interrupted it. Do not drift back.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But that is not the way you learned Christ.” After the bleak description of vv. 18–19, Paul turns on a dime. That world — darkened, alienated, callous, insatiable — is not what you signed up for. You learned something completely different.

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say “you learned about Christ” or “you learned Christ’s teaching.” He says you learned Christ — a Person, not a curriculum. In the ancient world you learned a philosopher’s ideas; the philosopher himself was just the delivery mechanism. Paul is saying something far more radical: the content of Christian learning is Christ himself. You were not handed a new moral code. You were introduced to a living Person — and knowing him is what changes everything.

This is the sharpest possible contrast with the futile mind of v. 17. The pagan mind drifts because it has no fixed point. The Christian mind has one: a Person who does not change, who is not a theory, who can be known and who makes himself known. That is what you learned. Live like it.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Assuming that you have heard him and were taught in him” — Paul is not doubting their conversion but reminding them what they received. And notice the little word: taught in him, not by him. Had he meant mere agency he could have said “through him.” He writes “in him” — the incorporative “in Christ” language that saturates this letter. The teaching did not arrive from outside as an information transfer, a parcel of facts handed over at arm’s length; it happened within your union with Christ. This is why the futile, darkened mind of vv.17–19 could never arrive here — it operates outside that union — and why what follows is not a new rulebook posted from a distance but instruction from inside the sphere of Christ, able to produce a “new self” (v.24) rather than one more round of futile effort.

“As the truth is in Jesus” — and again the exact words. Not that the truth is Jesus, an equals sign, but that it is in him: found, lodged, given a face in him. And Paul uses the human name deliberately — not “Christ” the title but “Jesus,” the man who walked in Galilee, touched lepers, was crucified under Pilate, and rose. Truth is not an abstract system floating free of a person; it has taken flesh in a specific human life. Hold that, for it sets the axis of the passage: the truth is in Jesus (v.21), the old self is corrupted through deceitful desires (v.22). Truth against deceit — that is the real contest. The old life is not merely naughty; it is a lie whispered to a man about where his happiness lies.

So when you want to know what truth looks like in flesh and blood — how to forgive, how to suffer — you do not consult a definition; you look at Jesus. You could hand a man the dictionary meaning of courage, accurate and bloodless, or point him to the soldier who threw himself on the grenade for his friends — courage with a face. A piano teacher can give you the theory of a sonata, or sit down and play it: “there — that is what it is meant to sound like.” In Jesus the truth about God and about what a human life was made to be stopped being a concept and became a life you can watch. The world says truth is whatever feels right to you; Paul says it is not ours to shape at all, because it is found in a Person who cannot be revised — “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Heb. 13:8; cf. 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put off” — the clothing image was already common in the ancient world, but Paul sharpens it: this is not adjusting your wardrobe but stripping off an entire identity — the whole of who you take yourself to be, your deepest loves and loyalties and habits. And “your old self” is literally “the old man” (as in Rom. 6:6; Col. 3:9) — not the body or the personality but the whole human self as it was before Christ, the person you were in Adam, oriented away from God. It is not a part of you; it is the old you.

Paul says this old self “belongs to your former manner of life,” and the phrasing is deliberate. The old self and the old life are so bound together that you cannot keep one and lose the other. The old way of living is the old self’s natural habitat; if you want to leave the old life behind, the old self must go with it. You cannot keep the old self and expect new behaviour — the root and the fruit come as a package.

And it is “corrupt” — not in the sense of dishonest, but rotting: the word for decay, something actively dying. You do not renovate what is rotting; you put it off. It is corrupting “through deceitful desires” — desires called deceitful because they make promises they cannot keep: this will satisfy you, this will fill the gap. They never do, and with each broken promise the person goes deeper in, feeding on what cannot nourish, slowly consuming himself. James names the lure exactly — each is “lured and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14) — and the believer’s answer is decisive: those who belong to Christ “have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between “put off” (v.22) and “put on” (v.24) stands the hinge: be renewed. Three things about it matter. It is continuous — not a one-off experience but a daily process that must keep happening. It is something done to you: “be renewed,” not “renew yourself” — God does the renewing, you receive it, which rules out both passivity and mere willpower (“work out your own salvation… for it is God who works in you,” Phil. 2:12–13). And it happens “in the spirit of your minds” — the mind’s governing centre, the deepest inner person; which is why behaviour cannot simply be commanded from outside, and why Paul says elsewhere, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Rom. 12:2).

Practically, you cannot manufacture this renewal, but you can pursue the means through which God gives it: Scripture that retrains the mind, prayer that opens the soul, honest community, the regular receiving of the preached word. To neglect these is not to be passive; it is to starve the very faculty God is renewing.

But take heart — this is a promise before it is a command. The renewing is God’s work, and “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Phil. 1:6). The change is often slow, and some days you will see no progress at all; yet the Spirit is transforming you “from one degree of glory to another” (2 Cor. 3:18). Think of John Newton — once the hard-hearted captain of a slave ship — whom God renewed not in a day but degree by degree over a lifetime, until that same mind gave the church “Amazing Grace.” Near the end, his memory nearly gone, he could still say: “I remember two things: that I am a great sinner, and that Christ is a great Saviour.” That is a renewed mind, and the God who did it for Newton is doing it for you. So do not measure the work by a single day (cf. Col. 3:10).

verseByVerse.quote: and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put on the new self” — the same clothing image, and Paul uses it elsewhere (“put on the Lord Jesus Christ,” Rom. 13:14; “put on the armour of God,” 6:11). Clothing implies a deliberate act: you do not accidentally get dressed. And this new self is “created after the likeness of God” — Paul reaching back to Genesis 1:26. This is what humanity was made for: to reflect God’s character. The fall defaced that image; in Christ it is being restored — not an improved old self but a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17). Yet it is more than Eden restored. Adam was innocent but not safe, untested and able to fall; the pattern of the new self is not the first Adam but the last (1 Cor. 15:45) — Christ, tried in every respect, obedient unto death, risen and beyond all falling. The destination is a Christlikeness that can never again be lost (Rom. 8:29).

It shows “in true righteousness and holiness” — righteousness leaning toward what we owe our neighbour (honesty, justice, love), holiness leaning Godward (reverence, consecration), and true meaning the genuine article, inward reality and not a mask.

How does a Christian actually do this? Paul’s silence is a clue — it is not complicated. To put on the new self is simply to act from who you now are in Christ, not who you used to be. Picture a child taken off the street and adopted into a noble house. His birth has not changed, but his belonging has, entirely. The old instincts linger — he hoards food, flinches at kindness, waits to be thrown out — and learning to “put on” his new self is nothing more than learning to live as what he now truly is: a son at his father’s table. He does not earn the sonship by behaving like a son; he behaves like a son because he already is one (Eph. 1:5). So in any moment — a conversation, a temptation — ask what the person you are in Christ would do, and do it by faith, before the feeling follows. Paul gives the concrete shape in the very next verses. And measure it by trajectory, not perfection: the adopted son still flinches, and is a son all the same; the question is which way you are facing, and whether, having fallen, you rise and walk on in the clothes your Father gave you (cf. Col. 3:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Now Paul lands the rubber on the road. Theology becomes Tuesday morning. Five commands, each grounded in the gospel, each aimed at the one thing that makes the body of Christ function or fail: the daily choices of ordinary people in ordinary relationships.

Tell the truth — because we are members of one another and a body cannot survive on false signals. Deal with anger before the sun goes down — because unresolved grievance is a beachhead the devil will occupy and you will not evict him easily once he is inside. Work and give — because the hands that once took are now instruments of grace. Speak only what builds — because your words can carry grace or corruption to the soul of the person who hears them. Forgive — as God in Christ forgave you. That last phrase is everything. The standard is not proportional. It is not “forgive reasonably.” It is: forgive the way the cross forgave you — absorbing the cost, releasing the debt, not because the other person has earned it but because you have been forgiven the unearnable.

Behind it all stands the Holy Spirit (v. 30) — not an impersonal force but a Person who can be grieved. He grieves at falsehood because he is the Spirit of truth. He grieves at unresolved bitterness because he is the bond of peace. He grieves at corrupting words because he is building a holy body. And the wonder: he grieves — and stays. This is the love that will not let go.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Grieving of the Spirit and the Ethics of Grace

Verse 30 — "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" — is one of the most searching statements in the New Testament about the nature of the Spirit. He can be grieved. This word (lupeō) in Greek means to cause sorrow, to wound. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force that responds mechanically to human sin; He is a Person with genuine emotional sensibility who is affected by the moral life of the community He inhabits. The sins Paul has listed — falsehood, uncontrolled anger, stealing, corrupting speech, bitterness, wrath, malice — do not merely harm the community; they wound the indwelling Guest.

The phrase "by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" provides the context for the warning. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who has sealed us for the final day — who is our guarantee of the inheritance (1:14), the deposit of our future glory. To grieve Him is therefore not a trivial matter; it is to harm the very relationship that is the ground of our assurance and the means of our transformation. This is not a threat to the believer's salvation; Paul does not say "by whom you were sealed unless you grieve Him." The sealing is certain. But the quality of the Spirit's presence and work in the community is affected by how the community lives.

The climactic command — "forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (v.32) — sets the standard for Christian forgiveness at the level of the cross: freely given, fully extended, without conditions. The Reformers consistently emphasised that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision — the decision to release the debt, to no longer hold the offence against the offender, to treat them as God treats us in Christ: with kindness and grace. This is impossible from human resources. It is possible only for those who have received it from God and draw on the same source to extend it to others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was, as we have noted, extraordinarily diverse. With diversity comes friction. The command against falsehood (v.25) — "speak truth with your neighbour, for we are members of one another" — addresses the social lubricant of deception that holds many human communities together. In the body of Christ, truth-telling is not optional; it is structurally necessary. A body in which the members lie to one another cannot function. The command against corrupting speech (v.29) — only what builds up — addresses the tongue that tears down, the word that diminishes, the comment that cuts. In a diverse community under pressure, these are the sins most likely to do lasting damage.

Now: "Do not let the sun go down on your anger" is one of the most practically demanding commands in Scripture, and one of the most consistently violated in married life, family life, and church life. We carry grievances. We nurse wounds. We let distance harden into walls. The apostle's word cuts through all of it: move toward resolution before night falls. This does not mean every conflict is resolved in an evening — some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work to heal. But the direction must always be toward each other, not away. The community that actually practices this — that refuses to let resentment calcify, that keeps short accounts, that forgives as God in Christ forgave — will be noticed. It will be extraordinary. It will be a sign of the Kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Having put away falsehood” — the form Paul uses describes something already done (or assumed done) as the basis for the command that follows: you put away falsehood in principle at conversion, when you put off the old self (v.22), and now must live consistently with that. It is the same logic as Romans 6: you have died to sin, so stop acting as though you haven’t. The putting away is real; the speaking of truth must now match it. And “falsehood” is more than outright lying — the word covers the full range of untruth: deliberate lies, yes, but also half-truths designed to mislead, flattery that says what people want to hear, silence when something honest needs to be said, and the careful management of how others see you. Falsehood is any communication meant to create a false impression, and Paul has shown (vv.17–19) that it belongs to the old life; to keep lying after putting on the new self is to reach back for the old rags.

“Speak the truth with his neighbour” means more than “don’t lie.” Paul is quoting Zechariah 8:16, so “neighbour” reaches to anyone you deal with — truth-telling is not merely an internal church standard — but he at once narrows the focus: “for we are members of one another,” the body of Christ. His primary concern is truth within the community, because lying to a fellow member is self-destructive, like one part of a body sending false signals to another; the body cannot function without honest communication between its parts. And to “speak truth” is to be the kind of person whose word can be trusted completely — who says the honest thing even when silence would be easier, keeps his word in small things and large, and is the same in private as in public. Truth is the oxygen the body of Christ runs on (cf. Zech. 8:16; Rom. 12:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Be angry, and do not sin.” The form is a command, like “speak truth” in v.25, but most read it as permission rather than obligation: not “you must be angry” but “when you are angry, that is permitted.” Paul is quoting Psalm 4:4, and his point is that anger itself is not sinful — there are things you should be angry about. Jesus was angry at the money-changers in the temple (John 2:15–16) and at the hardness of heart that preferred a rule over a man’s healing (Mark 3:5); God himself is described as angry at sin throughout Scripture. Anger at injustice, cruelty, or wickedness is a right and appropriate response; never to be angry at anything is not holiness but indifference.

So the sin is not the anger; the sin is what you do with it. Say a colleague takes credit for something you did: you feel angry, and that anger is legitimate, a response to a real injustice. But if you then tell everyone in the office what he did, or start quietly undermining him, or lie awake that night rehearsing it and adding to it — now the anger has crossed into sin. The anger was right; what it became was not. Which is why Paul adds, “do not let the sun go down on your anger”: deal with it before the day ends. He does not mean every conflict must be fully resolved by sunset — that is not always possible — but do not go to sleep still nursing it. Before the day closes, do something: go to the person if you can, or at the least release the anger to God in prayer, handing it over rather than carrying it into the next day. Anger nursed through the night hardens — what was a legitimate grievance in the evening becomes resentment by morning, and resentment by next week something darker still. Deal with it while it is still fresh and manageable (cf. Matt. 5:23–24; 18:15).

verseByVerse.quote: and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “and” here means “as a result”: this is the consequence of letting the sun go down on your anger. Do not give it overnight, because if you do, you hand the devil a foothold. The word (topos) means a place, a position — the image is a military beachhead, an opening inside your lines from which an enemy can operate. Paul is not being dramatic; he is being precise.

Picture two elders who disagree sharply over a decision. Words are exchanged; neither goes to the other to clear the air — it feels awkward, and the matter was technically settled. A week passes; they are polite on Sunday but something has cooled. Months later the congregation feels a tension in the leadership without quite naming it; people sense which elder they are more comfortable around; within a year there are two quiet camps. No one planned it. A small, unresolved anger was simply given time to harden, and the devil, who is in no hurry, used it.

The enemy does not need to tempt you into great sin if he can get you to leave a small wound unattended. That is all a foothold requires — so “that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Were there really thieves in the church? Evidently — Paul does not write hypothetically. These congregations were full of day-labourers, dock-workers, and household slaves living hand to mouth, and petty theft was woven into survival: pilfering from a master’s stores, skimming at the harbour, “forgetting” to return what was borrowed. The culture barely blinked; Paul does — in the body of Christ the common thing is no longer the acceptable thing.

Watch the shape of the command — three steps, and the third is the surprise. Stop stealing; work honestly instead; so that you may have something to give. The gospel never merely empties a life; it refills it, aimed the other way. The hand that once took becomes the hand that gives. As Begg notes, the cure for taking is not just keeping your hands to yourself — it is opening them. Zacchaeus got there in an afternoon: the tax-collector who took became, the day salvation came to his house, a man who gave half his goods away (Luke 19:8–9).

And though you have never burgled a house, the verse still lands close, for theft wears respectable clothes: the padded expense claim, the hours billed but not worked, the cash job kept off the books, the “borrowed” tools that never come home. The command is the same, and so is the surprise: God’s goal for a working life is not merely that it stays honest, but that the pay-packet becomes a channel — that there is margin, on purpose, for the person in need. In Christ, work stops being only how you get and becomes how you give; “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sapros — rotten, putrid, the word for decaying food. Speech that tears down, gossips, or belittles is as out of place in the body of Christ as rotting meat at a feast. And the standard Paul sets against it is high: every word good for building up, fitting the occasion, and — the phrase that deserves its own weight — “that it may give grace to those who hear.” The word is charis, the same grace Ephesians uses for God’s undeserved gift. Your words can be a vehicle of it: an honest encouragement to someone doubting, a gentle truth to someone drifting, a simple acknowledgement to someone who feels invisible — grace delivered through a human mouth.

The reverse is also true. Corrupting talk does not merely fail to give grace; it takes grace away — a careless word can undo in a moment what months of encouragement built, a piece of gossip poisons how others see someone before he enters the room. Hear it in a single case: two members learn that a third, James, has just lost his job. “Did you hear about James? I always thought he wasn’t cut out for that role” — possibly true, zero grace, and James is now worse off in the community than before those words. Or: “James has just lost his job and he’s shaken — could we pray for him now and someone reach out this week?” Same information; grace given; the body moves toward him rather than past him.

So the question over every word is not only “is this true?” but “does it build up? does it fit this moment? will the one who hears be richer for it, or poorer?” (cf. Prov. 15:23; Col. 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse arrives like a sudden change of key, and it is meant to. Paul has been speaking of words and community, and then, without warning, he pulls back the curtain and shows us who is in the room: the Holy Spirit himself, listening to every word, affected by every choice. It is the most personal possible motive for everything he has commanded. “Do not grieve” means to cause sorrow, to pain — the language of grief felt in close relationships. Paul is not saying the Spirit becomes angry or withdraws, or that you lose your salvation; he is saying something more intimate — the Spirit can be hurt. He is a Person, the third Person of the Trinity, not an impersonal force, and he feels relational grief when holiness is spurned by those he indwells.

How is he grieved? By the very things in these verses: falsehood, for he is “the Spirit of truth” (John 16:13); unresolved anger, for he is the bond of peace (4:3); corrupting speech, for he works to build up the body; bitterness, wrath, and slander (v.31), for they are the opposite of his fruit (Gal. 5:22–23). He is not grieved by weakness, failure, or honest struggle — these he meets with intercession (Rom. 8:26). He is grieved by wilful, unrepentant persistence in what Christ died to remove.

And the reason Paul gives is “by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” A seal in the ancient world marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity: this belongs to someone, and that someone stands behind it. The Spirit himself is the seal (1:13–14), God’s own mark of ownership and the down payment (arrabōn) on a redemption as certain as God himself. So the appeal is both warning and wonder. The warning: do not grieve the very Person who is your guarantee of glory, who holds your future and intercedes for you day by day. The wonder: he grieves — and stays. He is sealed to you as surely as you are sealed by him. His grief is the grief of a love that will not let go (cf. Isa. 63:10; 2 Cor. 1:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six words, laid down like a row of weapons to be surrendered — and each is distinct. Bitterness is the settled sourness of a soul that has been wounded and chosen to nurse the wound rather than release it — anger kept too long; it colours everything, and Hebrews 12:15 warns of a “root of bitterness” that springs up and “defiles many,” for its damage is never merely personal. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden hot flare, the outburst that leaves wreckage and does not think before it speaks (James 1:19–20). Anger (orgē) is its cold twin — settled, brooding resentment that builds a case, remembers every offence, and waits (the very thing v.26 warned about).

Clamour is anger gone public and lost its restraint — the raised voice that turns a disagreement into a scene, the moment a private grievance becomes a public fracture. Slander (blasphēmia) is injurious speech about another, whether false or maliciously true — the same root as blasphemy against God, and within the church it attacks the members of Christ’s body and so, in a real sense, Christ himself (Acts 9:4). And malice comes last because it is the root: a settled ill-will, the soil in which all the others grow. To put away malice is the most fundamental of the six — the call to have the heart itself transformed, not merely the behaviour managed.

And notice the anatomy, for we have seen it before. In v.18 a hardened heart darkened the understanding and issued at last in a ruined life. Here malice in the heart sours into bitterness, erupts as wrath and anger, and breaks out of the mouth as clamour and slander. Both times the road runs from the heart outward — and both times the cure must begin where the road begins (cf. 1 Pet. 2:1; Col. 3:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having stripped the wardrobe bare in v.31, Paul now furnishes it — three words, and the ground on which all three stand: as God in Christ forgave you. Kind (chrēstos) is practical, active goodness — the word was used of wine mellowed with age, no longer sharp; Jesus uses its root of his own “easy” yoke (Matt. 11:30). It looks for ways to be good to the people around you, especially the difficult ones. Tender-hearted (eusplagchnos) is literally “good-bowelled” — a heart genuinely moved by another’s pain, not sympathetic at a safe distance; it is the compassion of Christ himself, “moved with compassion” at human need (Matt. 9:36), and the very opposite of the hardened heart of v.18.

Forgiving (charizomenoi) carries the theological weight: it shares its root with charis, grace. To forgive is to grace someone — to give what they do not deserve and cannot earn. It is not excusing (pretending the wrong did not happen), nor is it reconciliation (which needs the other’s repentance and may take time); it is a unilateral decision of the wronged party to release the debt, to stop holding the offence as a claim. Why is it so hard? Because it feels like injustice — like letting the other off the hook. Which is exactly why Paul grounds it in the cross: as God in Christ forgave you. There the debt was not cancelled by pretending it did not exist; it was absorbed by the one who was wronged. God did not overlook sin; he paid for it himself. Christian forgiveness follows the same pattern — you absorb the cost rather than pass it on. That is not weakness; it is the most Christlike act a person can perform. And God is the standard for all three: kind (“the riches of his kindness,” Rom. 2:4), tender (“as a father shows compassion,” Ps. 103:13), forgiving at infinite cost. We are only passing on what we have already received.

Think how quietly it hides. Sarah fell out with Mark over a worship-team decision six months ago; he was dismissive, spoke sharply in front of others, never apologised. She serves beside him on Sundays but keeps her distance, answers his messages with bare courtesy, and has told two friends what happened — and tells herself she has forgiven him because she no longer thinks about it daily. Paul’s three words expose where she really is: the kindness gone, the tender-heartedness closed, the forgiveness incomplete — she has released the acute pain but kept the verdict. The way forward is not a feeling but a decision made in prayer at the foot of the cross: Lord, I release this. Mark owes me nothing. I received forgiveness I did not deserve; I extend the same. Then the behaviour follows — a genuine word toward him, an end to the quiet commentary, a willingness to be present rather than managed. It will not feel natural at first, and may need making again tomorrow.

And this is where the whole chapter has been going. The old clothes come off, the mind is renewed, the new clothes go on — not so we may admire ourselves in them, but because God has set his heart on presenting his people to himself “without spot or wrinkle… holy and without blemish” (5:27). Every truthful word, every anger surrendered before sundown, every hand that gives instead of takes, every debt released — these are the bride being made ready. He is not merely tidying our behaviour; he is dressing a bride for the day she sees her Husband’s face (cf. Rev. 19:7–8).

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 stakes out the great Reformed doctrine of the inseparability of justification and sanctification. The same grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make them righteous. Not simultaneously, not automatically — but inevitably. Where the root is real, the fruit will come. Paul’s commands in this chapter are not the conditions of acceptance; they are the evidence of it. The indicative always precedes and grounds the imperative.

The chapter also gives the church its most searching doctrine of common life. The body of Christ is not a collection of private spiritual journeys happening in the same building. It is an organism, with every member genuinely joined to every other — responsible for each other’s growth, dependent on each other’s gifts, harmed by each other’s sin. Falsehood in the body is not a private failure; it is a systemic wound. Unresolved anger is not a personal problem; it is a strategic opening for the enemy. This is the doctrine of the church made viscerally practical.

And at the centre stands the renewal of the mind — the hinge on which all change turns. Not willpower, not behaviour management, but transformation at the level where thinking happens. This is the Spirit’s sovereign work, received through the ordinary means of grace: the word, prayer, honest community, and obedience to what is already known. The Christian does not renew themselves. But they can position themselves daily in the hands of the One who does. cf. Rom. 12:1–2; 2 Cor. 3:18; Phil. 2:12–13.
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture saturated with the very patterns Paul describes in vv. 17–19 — a world of mystery religions, sexual licence, and moral relativism where the only sin was public embarrassment. To be told to “put off” this was not a minor adjustment; it was a complete reorientation of identity. And the alternative Paul offered — speaking truth, controlling anger, working honestly, forgiving freely — would have looked countercultural to the point of strangeness. The church in Ephesus was being asked to be a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The culture has changed; the pressure has not. The same patterns Paul named are alive and well: the mind drifting, the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more. The same temptations assault the same pressure points: to manage rather than truth-tell, to nurse grievance rather than forgive, to speak what entertains rather than what builds. And the same command stands: no longer walk as those who do not know God. Not because you must earn your standing — that is secured in Christ — but because you have been made new, and new creatures do not live in the old way.

You, reading this chapter on a Monday morning, can take one thing to work: the person sitting across from you is either a fellow member of the body or a neighbour made in God’s image. Either way, what you say matters, what you do with your anger matters, how you handle the truth matters. The renewal of the mind is not a mystical event. It is what happens when the Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of broods, speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one — and does it again tomorrow. This is how the body builds itself up in love.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.” The command is breathtaking in its scope, and its motivation is everything. We imitate God not because he is powerful or sovereign or even just — but because we are his beloved children, and children naturally, joyfully imitate those who love them. The motivation for holy living is not duty but delight, not fear but love, not the dread of punishment but the joy of resemblance.

The specific attribute to be imitated is love — but immediately defined by the cross: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, “a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (v. 2). This phrase reaches deep into the Old Testament sacrificial system. The “fragrant offering” (reah nichoach) was the language of divine acceptance — from Genesis 8:21 through the Levitical offerings, whenever God declared himself pleased with the sacrifice. Christ’s self-giving is the final, fully accepted offering that all those animal sacrifices could only foreshadow: freely given (prosphora) and enormously costly (thysia). The Father smells the fragrance and is satisfied. Wrath propitiated, covenant restored, the guilty declared righteous. This is the love to be imitated: cross-shaped, self-giving, asking not “what do I get?” but “what does this person need and what will it cost me to give it?”

Against this backdrop Paul names what does not belong: sexual immorality (porneia — the full range of sexual activity outside the marriage covenant; sex as a covenant act mirroring Christ and the church, too sacred to be treated as casual), impurity (akatharsia — broader than overt act, covering the imagination and desire not yet expressed; the inner life matters to God as much as the outer), and covetousness (pleonexia — the insatiable craving for more, the desire that places a created thing in the throne that belongs to God alone, which is why Paul calls it idolatry in v. 5). Covetousness must be distinguished from wise stewardship: providing for a household, prudent financial planning, and enjoying God’s good gifts are not covetousness. The diagnostic questions are: what is driving it? where is the heart set? does it produce generosity or hoarding? The root of covetousness is a failure of trust — a rival religion, the worship of More in place of the God who is enough.

The warning of verses 5–6 is sobering — those who practice these things without repentance have no inheritance in the kingdom. But a pastoral word is essential: Paul is describing a settled, unrepentant pattern of life, not the experience of the believer who struggles, falls, grieves, and returns. The evidence of genuine faith is not the absence of struggle but the presence of grief over sin and the refusal to make peace with what Christ died to remove. The dangerous condition is not the fall but the cessation of struggle — listening to the “empty words” of v. 6 and reclassifying sin as not-sin. For the one who is genuinely fighting: “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). A bruised reed he will not break (Isa. 42:3).
verseByVerse.theology:
Cruciform Love as the Pattern of the Christian Life

"A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (v.2) — Paul's description of Christ's self-giving at the cross is drawn directly from the Old Testament sacrificial language. The burnt offering was described as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" (Leviticus 1:9; 8:21) — a sacrifice that God receives with satisfaction, that expresses the proper worship of creature before Creator. Paul applies this language to the cross: the death of Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, the perfect offering, the worship that satisfied the holiness of God and secured the salvation of His people.

The implication for ethics is profound: to walk in love in imitation of Christ is to participate in a form of worship. Every act of genuine, self-giving love — every moment of costly service, every forgiveness extended at personal cost, every preference of another's need over one's own comfort — is offered to God as a fragrant offering. The Christian life is not divided into sacred acts (prayer, church attendance) and secular acts (daily life, work, relationships). All of it is worship. The love that looks like Calvary, lived out in the ordinary texture of daily life, is received by God as the aroma of Christ Himself.

Covetousness is identified in v.5 as idolatry — a striking identification that requires reflection. Covetousness is not merely wanting what others have; it is the orientation of the heart toward things rather than toward God, treating the creature as the source of satisfaction rather than the Creator. In this sense it is the root of sexual immorality as well: the sexualised culture is a culture of covetousness, of insatiable appetite, of treating persons as objects to be consumed. The gospel addresses this at the root by offering the only love that actually satisfies — the love of God in Christ, which surpasses knowledge and fills the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: "Be imitators of God" — in the Greco-Roman world, this language had a specific resonance. The mystery religions and philosophical schools both spoke of homoiōsis theō — likeness to God — as the goal of the spiritual life. But the path they offered was typically ascetic withdrawal, esoteric knowledge, ritual elevation. Paul offers a radically different path: imitate the God who descended, who gave Himself up, who went to the cross for His enemies. The divine pattern to be imitated is not the god on the Olympian heights, remote and powerful, but the God who came down in love and poured Himself out in death. The imitation called for is not upward escape but downward love.

Now: Sexual immorality has been rebranded in our age as liberation, as authentic self-expression, as the natural pursuit of desire. Covetousness is marketed as aspiration, ambition, the engine of economic progress. Paul's gospel cuts through all of it — not with a longer list of prohibitions, but with a higher vision. You are a beloved child of the God who gave His Son for you. You have been loved with a love that went to the cross. Now walk in that love: freely, lavishly, cruciformly, without counting the cost. This is not the moralism of a killjoy god; it is the invitation of a Father who wants His children to look like Him and to know the joy of doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mimētai tou theou — imitators of God. The Greek word gives us “mime.” A child mimics a parent in play; the grown child imitates a father in earnest. This is Paul’s call — not to copy a set of rules but to watch the Father and do likewise.

The ground of the command is everything: “as beloved children”. We imitate God not to earn his favour but because we already have it. The motivation is love received, not performance demanded. A child who is secure in a father’s love naturally wants to be like him. That is the dynamic Paul is describing. cf. Matt. 5:48; 1 John 3:1–3.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The standard of love is the cross. Christ loved us and gave himself up — voluntarily, at infinite personal cost, for our benefit and not his own. This is the pattern: not sentiment, not natural affection, but cross-shaped love that asks not “what do I get?” but “what does this person need, and what will it cost me to give it?” And Paul calls it “a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God,” reaching into the deep language of the Old Testament sacrificial system. A “fragrant offering” (rêah nîchôach) was the phrase used when God declared himself pleased with a sacrifice — when the offering was accepted and the worshipper received; it runs through Leviticus and Numbers, appearing first at Noah’s altar after the flood (Gen. 8:21). It is the language of divine acceptance: the sacrifice has reached God, God is satisfied, the relationship is right.

Paul applies that whole weight to the cross. Every animal sacrifice in Israel’s history was pointing toward this one moment; where repeated sacrifices could never finally deal with sin (Heb. 10:1–4), Christ’s offering was the one, fully accepted, once-for-all sacrifice — “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Heb. 10:14). The Father smelled the fragrance and was satisfied; the wrath was absorbed; the broken relationship restored. Two words deepen the picture: prosphora (offering) stresses the voluntariness — Christ was not seized but gave himself (John 10:18) — and thysia (sacrifice) stresses the cost, the actual giving of life. Freely given and enormously costly, neither to be separated from the other. And this is what Paul holds before us as the pattern for how we love one another: the cross is not only the ground of our salvation but the shape of our lives (cf. 1 John 3:16; Heb. 10:1–14).

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three vices — sexual immorality (porneia), impurity (akatharsia), and covetousness (pleonexia) — are not merely to be avoided but “not even named among you, as is proper among saints.” The standard is identity, not just morality: what defiles has no place in the set-apart community. Porneia is broad — every sexual act outside the marriage covenant of a man and a woman, pornography included (the words share a root). Not because the body is evil (it is God’s and Christ’s, 1 Cor. 6:19–20), but because sexual union is a covenant act that mirrors the union of Christ and the church (5:31–32); to treat it as casual is to desecrate a sacrament. Akatharsia reaches wider — the inner life of desire, the imagination fed on what degrades; the look of lust is already the act in the heart (Matt. 5:28).

Pleonexia is literally “the desire to have more” — the insatiable craving for more money, status, comfort, pleasure, driven not by need but by an appetite that cannot be filled. Paul places it beside sexual sin because the dynamic is the same: wanting what God has not given, and enthroning a craving where God belongs — which is why in v.5 he calls it idolatry.

But covetousness is not the same as faithfulness. Providing for your household is a duty, not greed (1 Tim. 5:8); wise saving and planning is commended (the ant, Prov. 6:6–8; Joseph storing grain, Gen. 41); enjoying God’s good gifts — a home, a meal, a holiday — is gratitude, for he “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Tim. 6:17); and honest ambition is not sin. The line runs through the heart. Ask: what is driving it — love and responsibility, or an appetite never satisfied, that upgrades and immediately eyes the next upgrade? Where is the treasure set — held open-handed as a trust, or clutched as security and identity, so that losing it would be devastation (Matt. 6:21)? And does it produce generosity or hoarding, for the true steward who plans well also gives well (2 Cor. 9:6–8)? At bottom, covetousness is a failure of trust — the quiet belief that God cannot be relied on to provide, that security must be seized rather than received. That is why Paul names it a rival religion: the worship of More in place of the God who is enough (cf. Luke 12:15–21; Heb. 13:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary: The catalog moves from deeds to words: filthiness, foolish talk, crude joking. The Greco-Roman world celebrated wit and bawdy humor; Paul marks it as “out of place” in the community of the cross. The antidote is striking: not solemn silence but thanksgiving. Gratitude is the natural speech of those who know what they have been given. A heart full of genuine thanksgiving has no room for talk that degrades; it overflows with praise. The same Greek word (eucharistia, thanksgiving) gives us “Eucharist” — the name many Christian traditions use for the Lord’s Supper or Communion, the meal of remembrance and thanksgiving at the heart of Christian worship. The connection is deliberate: the table where we remember what Christ gave us is meant to shape everything we say away from that table. A mouth full of genuine gratitude for the cross has little room left for the words Paul just listed.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names the root of his warnings: sexual immorality and covetousness are not merely moral failures but idolatry — the covetous has made possession his god, the immoral has made pleasure his, worship aimed at the wrong object (Rom. 1:25; Col. 3:5). And such a person “has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” — his most solemn language: not a lesser blessing withheld, but exclusion from the kingdom entirely.

But many true believers struggle with exactly these sins — does this mean they are not saved? Two truths must be held together. First, Paul is describing a pattern of life, not a moment of failure. The Greek participles are ongoing: the person who is immoral, who is covetous, as a settled, unrepentant way of living. He is not describing the believer who falls, grieves, confesses, and fights. And 1 Corinthians 6 makes the same list and then adds the decisive words: “and such were some of you” — past tense. The one who has truly come to Christ has been washed; his direction has changed, even if the struggle has not ended.

Second, the struggle itself is the evidence of new life. The person who falls into sin and is devastated, who hates it in himself and longs to be free — that person is not the one Paul warns; the unregenerate does not wage war against his sin, he makes peace with it. Romans 7 gives the believer’s cry: “wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me?” That anguish is not the voice of the kingdom-excluded but of one who belongs to Christ and knows he is not yet what he will be. The mark of the unbeliever is not that he sins but that he does not fight; the mark of the believer is not that he never falls but that he cannot stay down. So if this verse troubles you, that trouble is itself a sign of life — the person Paul warns is not troubled at all (cf. 1 Cor. 6:9–11; Rom. 7:24–8:1; 1 John 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let no one deceive you with empty words.” These are the sophistries that minimise the stakes: God is gracious, these things don’t really matter; everyone struggles with this; a loving God would never judge. Paul calls them lies — for it is “because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience,” not arbitrary punishment but the settled, holy opposition of a righteous God to all that destroys his image-bearers.

And a word for the believer who reads vv.5–6 and feels the ground give way — who knows his own heart, struggles seriously with temptation, and now reads no inheritance in the kingdom. Read it with the whole of Scripture. The distinction is not between the sinless and the sinful — there are no sinless people this side of glory — but between those walking in the light and those walking in darkness (1 John 1:5–9). The one who falls and is grieved, who confesses and returns, who hates the sin and longs to be free, is not described by v.5 but by 1 John 1:9: “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive.” What Paul warns against is different — the person who has stopped fighting, reclassified his sin as not-sin, and settled into unrepentant practice while keeping a Christian name. That is the danger: not the fall, but the refusal to get up.

So if you are struggling — genuinely grieved, wanting to be free — hear the word that stands over all Paul’s warnings: “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). The blood of Christ is sufficient for every sin you have committed and will commit; the Spirit who grieves over your sin (4:30) also intercedes for you with groanings too deep for words (Rom. 8:26). You are not beyond reach. Keep fighting, keep confessing, keep returning (cf. Ps. 51:17; Isa. 42:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary: “Therefore” draws the conclusion from the gravity of vv. 5–6: because these works bring wrath, and because the community belongs to the kingdom of light (v. 8), a clear distinction must be maintained. “Do not become partners” — do not enter fellowship or complicity in these works. This is not an instruction to social isolation from unbelievers but a refusal to participate in the practices that belong to the old age. The church cannot be the church and also share in the works of darkness without fundamental self-contradiction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." The sharpness of this contrast arrests us every time we read it. Not "you were in darkness" — you were darkness itself. Not "you are now in the light" — you are light. The transformation is total, ontological, irreversible. Something has changed at the deepest level of what you are, not merely where you are or what you do. And the imperative that follows — "walk as children of light" — is not a command to achieve something new but to express something already true. Be in your behaviour what you are in your nature. Let the outside match the inside.

Light bears fruit. The fruit of light is "in all goodness and righteousness and truth" (v.9) — three qualities that together describe the character of the God who is light (1 John 1:5). The child of light is not defined primarily by what they avoid but by what they produce: genuine moral goodness, the rightness of life aligned with God's law and character, the transparency of truth-telling in every dimension of life. This fruit is not manufactured by effort; it grows naturally from a nature that has been fundamentally changed. Light cannot help but produce light-fruits.

And light exposes what darkness conceals. The children of light do not retreat from the darkness of the culture (withdrawal) or blend into it (accommodation). They expose it — by the simple, consistent, visible presence of a life lived in the open before God. This exposure is not aggressive or confrontational; it does not require denunciation or political engagement (though these may have their place). It requires holiness. "When anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible" (v.13). The most prophetic thing the church can do in a dark age is simply to be genuinely, visibly, persistently light.
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, Darkness, and the Prophetic Witness of Holiness

The ontological language of this passage — "you were darkness," "you are light" — reflects the radical nature of regeneration. The new birth is not a moral improvement programme; it is a change of nature. What was dark has become light. What was oriented toward self and sin has been reoriented toward God and holiness. This is the consistent teaching of the Reformed tradition: regeneration is sovereign, total, and irreversible — a work of God in the interior of the person that creates a new appetite, a new orientation, a new capacity for the things of God.

The call to "take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them" (v.11) raises the question of the church's relationship to culture. The Reformed tradition has generally resisted both the temptation to total withdrawal (a pietism that disengages from the world) and the temptation to total accommodation (a liberalism that conforms to it). The middle path — engagement without assimilation, presence without compromise — is what it means to be light in the world. The church that is genuinely, visibly holy is not only doing something good for its own members; it is doing something necessary for the world, exposing by contrast what the world cannot see about itself.

The awakening hymn of v.14 — "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" — is widely thought to be an early Christian baptismal hymn. It captures the eschatological urgency of the whole passage: the world is asleep, the darkness is presenting itself as normal and comfortable, and the church is called to be the community of the awakened, the risen, the enlightened. Not by shouting but by shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The darkness Paul describes in v.12 — "the things they do in secret" — was not merely a moral category. Ephesus had a fully developed underground of occult practice, of ritual darkness, of things done in the night that could not bear the daylight. The mystery religions operated precisely in the realm of secrets, of hidden things, of initiation into darkness. The church's commitment to transparency — to lives that could be lived fully in the open before God — was itself a form of witness against the culture of secrecy. You have nothing to hide because you have nothing to fear. You live in the light because Christ has shone on you.

Now: "Awake, O sleeper" has the ring of an alarm clock going off in a dark room. The world is sleeping — comfortable in its darkness, unaware of its danger, presenting its way of life as simply the normal and natural way to live. The church is called to wake up and to be awake — to see the world as it really is in the light of God's word, to live accordingly, and thereby to be the kind of community whose quality of life is itself an invitation: come and see what happens when Christ shines on you. In a culture that is drowsy with distraction and numbed by comfort, the church's wakefulness is among its most urgent callings.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice what Paul does not say. Not that they were in darkness and are now in light, but that they were darkness and are light — a change of nature, not merely of location. The very substance of what they are has been transformed by union with Christ. So “walk as children of light”: the indicative becomes the imperative. You do not walk in the light to become light; you walk as light because you already are it.

And these are not categories of ignorance and knowledge, as though education were the answer — they are moral and spiritual, and run deep in Scripture. Darkness is a life oriented away from God, with no living connection to him: the moral compass broken, so that what is evil looks acceptable and what is shameful is done without shame (v.12). It is the habitat of the old self of chapter 4 — the hardened heart, the calloused conscience — and the domain where the powers of 6:12 operate. And before Christ, Paul says bluntly, you were not merely in it; you were it. Light is its opposite in every dimension: a life oriented toward God, sharing his nature, for “God is light and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5) and Christ is the light of the world (John 8:12). The compass is restored; the hidden things that thrive in darkness cannot survive in you as they once did, because light exposes them.

So darkness is not just “being bad”; it is being without God, in a condition where you cannot even see clearly enough to know how lost you are. And light is not just “being better”; it is being joined to the One who is light, so that his nature begins to show in yours. What Paul describes is not moral improvement but a new identity (cf. Col. 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parenthesis defines what light naturally produces: goodness (moral excellence), righteousness (right relating to others), and truth (integrity, correspondence with reality) — not rules to perform but fruit to bear, the natural produce of a life transformed into light. Then Paul says “try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord,” and the verb rewards a pause. It is dokimazein — to test, examine, approve after careful evaluation, the word used for assaying metal to see whether it is genuine. Paul normally issues direct commands — do this, stop that, put off, put on — but here he does not say “obey this list.” He says: discern.

Why? Because the Christian life cannot be reduced to a rulebook. Rules cover the cases the lawmaker anticipated; life constantly produces situations no rulebook has addressed. What Paul calls for is deeper than compliance — the cultivated ability to read a situation in the light of knowing Christ and ask, what would please him here? That requires a mind renewed (4:23), a conscience sensitive to the Spirit, and a growing knowledge of what God values; in short, wisdom, which is exactly what the next section (vv.15–17) is about. The same verb appears in Romans 12:2 — “be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God” — with the same logic: the renewed mind does not just follow instructions but develops the capacity to perceive. Paul is describing moral maturity, not mere compliance: the goal is not a Christian who does right because he was told to, but one so formed by Christ that he can see what is right for himself (cf. Phil. 1:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Unfruitful works of darkness” — fruitlessness is the mark of the old life; where the fruit of light is good, right, and true, the works of darkness bear nothing that survives. The command is not only to abstain but to expose — rebuke, convict, bring into the open. This does not require lurid description; v. 12 notes that what is done in secret is too shameful even to name. Exposure happens through contrast: the sheer presence of lives lived in light makes darkness visible without needing to enumerate its contents in detail.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The logic is arresting: when light exposes darkness, the exposed thing becomes light — transformed by the very exposure that reveals it. This is true both of the conversion of sinners and the purification of the community. Think of a believer who has carried a hidden sin for years, something never told to anyone; the weight has not lifted but grown. The moment it is finally brought into the light — confessed to God, to a trusted friend, to a pastor — the grip weakens. Not because confession is magic, but because light has entered where darkness had been living undisturbed: the shame decreases, freedom to draw near returns, healing begins. Exposure is not merely an unmasking; it is the beginning of transformation. Light does not only reveal — it changes what it touches.

The hymn fragment of v.14 — “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” — is introduced by “for it says,” Paul’s usual formula for quoting Scripture, yet these exact words appear nowhere in the Old Testament. Most likely it is an early Christian hymn — sung, many scholars think, at baptisms, where the one rising from the water was called to “arise” from death into the light of Christ — a hymn that itself distils the Old Testament’s resurrection-and-light imagery (Isa. 26:19, “your dead shall live… awake and sing”; 60:1, “arise, shine, for your light has come”). Paul cites it as an evangelistic call to the sleeper who has not yet risen into Christ’s light — the very language of resurrection he has used for salvation throughout the letter (2:1–6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil." The third walk imperative carries a quality of urgency that is eschatological in character. The Christian does not live in a neutral moment; they live in a moment freighted with significance, in days that are evil (and therefore time-limited in their evil), in a window of opportunity that will not remain open forever. Wisdom means seeing this clearly and acting accordingly — not frantic and anxious, but alert and intentional, making the most of every opportunity because the Kingdom has come and its King is returning.

The contrast Paul draws between drunkenness and fullness of the Spirit is one of the most theologically provocative contrasts in the letter.
